title: Greedy Best-First: Porto Streets, Fast Decisions!
description: Watch Greedy Best-First sprint through Porto’s street graph using only the heuristic to pick the next best-looking intersection. The visualization reveals how “closer to the goal” can race ahead—sometimes sacrificing optimality for speed.
ig_caption:
🚦✨ **Greedy Best-First in Porto (Miragaia)!** ✨🚦

In this reel, we run **Greedy Best-First** on a real street-style **graph**: intersections are nodes, road segments are edges, and the algorithm always expands the node that looks most promising. 🧠📍

🔍 **Core idea (graph theory):**
We maintain a priority queue ordered purely by a heuristic **h(n)** (e.g., estimated distance from node *n* to the goal). Unlike A*, we don’t explicitly balance cost-so-far—so the search is “goal-directed” but can get trapped by locally attractive routes. ⚡

📌 **What you’re seeing:**
As the greedy frontier advances, it tends to follow the heuristic gradient—great for fast paths, but it may miss the globally shortest route when the map has curves, one-way quirks, or detours. 🗺️➡️

👀 Try this: pause on the moment it commits to a promising street—then imagine how changing the heuristic reshapes the entire exploration. 🔄

👉 Want a version using A* (or Dijkstra) on the same map next? Comment your pick and follow for more real-map algorithm visuals! 💬
fb_caption:
🚙💡 **Porto + Greedy Best-First pathfinding!** 💡🚙

This visualization turns real street layouts into a **graph search problem**: intersections become nodes and roads become edges. **Greedy Best-First** expands the node with the smallest heuristic distance to the goal, which can produce quick routes—but may not always guarantee the shortest path.

📣 If you like learning-by-seeing, share this with a friend who loves algorithms, and tell us in the comments: should we compare it next with **A*** or **Dijkstra** on the same city graph?
